Reference / fs/path

fs/path#

Purely lexical paths for native and foreign path grammars.

Version: v1.0.0

Synopsis#

let native = Path("var").child("log").child("app.log");
let foreign = Path("C:\\Users\\alice", PathStyle.windows);

Description#

Purely lexical paths for native and foreign path grammars.

Path(text) interprets text using the current platform. Pass PathStyle only when working with a path belonging to another platform:

Path(parts...) is the portable application-facing join. It asks the runtime for the current platform and never makes callers choose a separator:

let config = Path("etc", "okkama", "config.toml");

A later absolute part replaces everything accumulated before it. Joining, parent lookup and absolute detection never consult the filesystem and never resolve symlinks or ... The paths they make are tidied: a . segment and a repeated separator go away, so Path("a/./b").child("c") is a/b/c.

Public API#

enum PathStyle#

enum PathStyle = (posix, windows)

Which platform's grammar a path follows: separators, roots, drive letters.

PathStyle.posix#

posix

PathStyle.windows#

windows

object Path#

object Path does Comparing<Path>

A path as names, worked out by the text alone: the disk is never asked.

Path.Path#

Path(origin is string)

A path in this platform's grammar: Path("var/log/app.log").

Path.Path#

Path(origin is string, style is PathStyle)

A path in another platform's grammar: Path("C:\\Users", PathStyle.windows).

Path.Path#

Path(parts is ...string)

The parts joined with this platform's separator: Path("etc", "okkama", "config.toml"); a later absolute part replaces what came before.

Path.parent#

parent() is Path

The path without its last name; the root's parent is the root.

Path.child#

child(part is string) is Path

This path with one more name: Path("var").child("log").

Path.name#

name() is string

The last part: Path("var/log/app.log").name() is "app.log"; "" for a root.

Path.absolute#

absolute() is bool

Whether the path starts at a root.

Path.parts#

parts() is @string

The names of the path, after the root of an absolute one: Path("/srv/app/a.log").parts() is ["/", "srv", "app", "a.log"], and Path("docs/guide.md").parts() is ["docs", "guide.md"]. . and repeated separators go away, .. stays.

Path.stem#

stem() is string

The name without its extension: "guide" for guide.md, "archive.tar" for archive.tar.gz; a name without an extension (notes, .bashrc) stays whole.

Path.extension#

extension() is string

What follows the last dot of the name, without the dot: "md" for guide.md. It is "" when the name has no dot, starts with its only dot (.bashrc) or ends with one (notes.).

Path.extension_replaced#

extension_replaced(extension is string) is Path

The path with another extension: Path("docs/guide.md").extension_replaced("html") is docs/guide.html, "" removes the extension, and a name without one gains it. A leading dot ("html" or ".html") is optional.

Path.relative_to#

relative_to(base is Path) is Path

The path from base to this one, by the names alone: Path("/srv/app/logs").relative_to(Path("/srv")) is app/logs, and a path relative to itself is ".". A path outside base, or of another grammar, is refused. Names compare exactly.

Path.normalized#

normalized() is Path

. and .. resolved by the names alone, without asking the disk: Path("a/./b/../c").normalized() is a/c. A .. above the root of an absolute path goes away; one above the start of a relative path stays.

Path.order#

order(other is Path) is Order

Orders paths by their text, for sorting.

Path.string#

string() is string

The path as text, with this path's separators.

Path.Grammar#

cap Grammar { style is PathStyle }

The lexical grammar, without probing the host filesystem.

Path.Grammar.style#

style is PathStyle
